title: Generic broken lines through finite hyperplane arrangements
statement: Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space [def-weil-vector-space-dimension], with its usual finite-dimensional topology, and let $\mathcal H$ be a finite set of distinct affine hyperplanes in $E$ (translates of linear subspaces of codimension one). Put $E_{\mathrm{reg}}=E\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal H}H$. Then $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$ meets every nonempty open subset of $E$. If $U\subseteq E$ is nonempty, open and convex, and $x,y\in U\cap E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, there is $z\in U\cap E_{\mathrm{reg}}$ such that the broken line $[x,z]\cup[z,y]$ meets no intersection $H\cap H'$ for distinct $H,H'\in\mathcal H$. Each of its two segments meets each hyperplane at most once, and each meeting is in the interior of that segment and crosses from one strict side to the other. In particular the broken line gives a finite sequence of components of $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$ from the component of $x$ to the component of $y$, with each consecutive pair separated by just one hyperplane at a point lying on no other hyperplane. If $\dim E=0$, the arrangement is empty and the constant path is allowed. Here $[u,v]=\{(1-t)u+tv:0\leq t\leq1\}$, convex means containing these segments between its points, and a component is a maximal connected subset.

source.place: Appendix C.8--C.10, printed pp.609--610, and C.19--C.22, pp.611--612, chamber geometry. Agent supporting lemma for the omitted root-system compatibility input of Conrad Theorem 6.2.4, printed p.202; not an assertion quoted verbatim from Milne. proof.text: For each $H$, choose a basis of its direction subspace $V_H$, extend it by one vector to a basis of $E$, and let $\ell_H$ be the coordinate functional of that last vector. If $a_H\in H$, put $f_H(u)=\ell_H(u-a_H)$. Then $\ell_H\ne0$, $H=f_H^{-1}(0)$, and $f_H((1-t)u+tv)=(1-t)f_H(u)+tf_H(v)$. By [lem-sfb-finite-dimensional-linear-map-continuous], applied over the complete nontrivially normed field $\mathbf R$, each $\ell_H$ is continuous; translation makes $f_H$ continuous. The two strict sides of $H$ are $f_H>0$ and $f_H<0$. The basis and codimension conventions are those of [def-weil-vector-space-dimension]. If $\dim E=0$, there can be no codimension-one subspace, hence no hyperplane; $E$ is a singleton and the constant path proves the conclusion. In the remaining steps allow the arrangement to be empty in positive dimension.

source.place: Appendix C.8--C.10 and C.19--C.22, printed pp.609--612, chamber geometry; agent supporting finite-affine-arrangement argument, not a quoted theorem of Milne.

proof.text: First prove density. If $\mathcal H$ is empty the assertion is immediate. Otherwise apply [lem-pc-finite-linear-avoidance] over the infinite field $\mathbf R$ to the proper linear subspaces $\ker\ell_H$, obtaining $v$ with $\ell_H(v)\ne0$ for every $H$. For a nonempty open set $O$, choose $q\in O$. Since $t\mapsto q+tv$ is continuous, $q+tv\in O$ for all $t$ in some interval $(-\epsilon,\epsilon)$. The equation $f_H(q+tv)=f_H(q)+t\ell_H(v)=0$ excludes just one value of $t$ for each $H$. An interval contains more than any prescribed finite number of distinct real numbers, so choose $t$ excluding this finite list. Then $q+tv\in O\cap E_{\mathrm{reg}}$. This proves the first assertion directly from linear avoidance and the displayed affine equation.

source.place: Appendix C.8--C.10 and C.19--C.22, printed pp.609--612, chamber geometry; agent supporting finite-affine-arrangement argument, not a quoted theorem of Milne.

proof.text: For each distinct pair $H,H^{\prime}$ with nonempty intersection, and $p=x$ or $y$, set $g_{p,H,H^{\prime}}(u)=f_H(p)f_{H^{\prime}}(u)-f_{H^{\prime}}(p)f_H(u)$. Its linear part is $m_{p,H,H^{\prime}}=f_H(p)\ell_{H^{\prime}}-f_{H^{\prime}}(p)\ell_H$, which is nonzero. Indeed both coefficients are nonzero since $p$ is regular. If $m=0$, then $\ell_{H^{\prime}}=c\ell_H$ with $c=f_{H^{\prime}}(p)/f_H(p)$. At a common point $a\in H\cap H^{\prime}$ both affine functions vanish, so $f_{H^{\prime}}(u)=\ell_{H^{\prime}}(u-a)=c\ell_H(u-a)=cf_H(u)$ for every $u$; this would give $H^{\prime}=H$. Pairs with empty intersection impose no condition. Thus there are only finitely many additional nonzero linear parts $m$.

source.place: Appendix C.8--C.10 and C.19--C.22, printed pp.609--612, chamber geometry; agent supporting finite-affine-arrangement argument, not a quoted theorem of Milne.

proof.text: If the finite list consisting of all $\ell_H$ and all $m_{p,H,H^{\prime}}$ is empty, take $z=x$. Otherwise [lem-pc-finite-linear-avoidance], applied to their kernels, gives $v$ on which all are nonzero. Choose $q\in U$ and $\epsilon>0$ such that $q+tv\in U$ for $|t|<\epsilon$. Each equation $f_H(q+tv)=0$ or $g_{p,H,H^{\prime}}(q+tv)=0$ excludes exactly one parameter, by its nonzero linear part on $v$. Choose $t$ in this interval outside the finite list and set $z=q+tv$. Then $z\in U\cap E_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and all $g_{p,H,H^{\prime}}(z)\ne0$. Convexity puts both segments inside $U$. If $(1-s)p+sz$ belonged to $H\cap H^{\prime}$, regularity of $p$ gives $s>0$, and the two zero equations imply $s g_{p,H,H^{\prime}}(z)=0$, a contradiction. Reversing the segment with $p=y$ gives the required avoidance for $[z,y]$ as well.

source.place: Appendix C.8--C.10 and C.19--C.22, printed pp.609--612, chamber geometry; agent supporting finite-affine-arrangement argument, not a quoted theorem of Milne.

proof.text: For either oriented segment $[u,v]=[x,z]$ or $[z,y]$, $f_H(u)$ and $f_H(v)$ are nonzero. The affine expression $(1-s)f_H(u)+sf_H(v)$ is either a nonzero constant, or has at most one zero. A zero in $[0,1]$ must have $0<s<1$; it is possible only when the endpoint values have opposite signs, and then its nonzero slope changes sign across the zero. Hence each meeting is a unique interior crossing. This also covers $u=v$: a constant segment with regular endpoint meets no hyperplane. The statement is per segment; a hyperplane can be crossed once on each leg.

source.place: Appendix C.8--C.10 and C.19--C.22, printed pp.609--612, chamber geometry; agent supporting finite-affine-arrangement argument, not a quoted theorem of Milne.

proof.text: For a choice of signs $\sigma_H\in\{1,-1\}$, write $C_\sigma=\{u:\sigma_H f_H(u)>0\text{ for every }H\}$. This set is convex by the affine formula, and when nonempty is connected by [lem-sfb-convex-set-connected]. A connected subset $A\subseteq E_{\mathrm{reg}}$ cannot contain both a point with $f_H>0$ and one with $f_H<0$: these two relatively open sets would give a disjoint nonempty open partition of $A$. Their relative openness follows from [lem-sfb-finite-dimensional-linear-map-continuous] as in step 1. Thus $A$ has a fixed sign for every $H$, and lies in a single $C_\sigma$. Each nonempty $C_\sigma$ is therefore a maximal connected subset, and these sets are exactly the components. In particular the signs determine the component, rather than merely labelling a subset of it.

source.place: Appendix C.8--C.10 and C.19--C.22, printed pp.609--612, chamber geometry; agent supporting finite-affine-arrangement argument, not a quoted theorem of Milne.

proof.text: Parameterize the two legs consecutively, and sort their finitely many crossing parameters. None occurs at $x,z,y$, and two different hyperplanes never have the same crossing point on a leg, by step 4. Between successive crossing parameters every $f_H$ has fixed sign by its affine formula; at the bend the signs agree because $z$ is regular. Step 6 therefore assigns one component to each successive portion. At each crossing precisely the sign of the crossed hyperplane changes. To see the local separation explicitly, let $w$ be that crossing point on $H$. For every $H^{\prime}\ne H$, $f_{H^{\prime}}(w)\ne0$, so by continuity and finiteness there is a neighbourhood of $w$ in $U$ on which all those signs stay fixed. On its two sides of $H$ lie exactly the two components just encountered. This gives the stated finite sequence from the component of $x$ to that of $y$. With no crossings it is a one-term sequence.
